chunks.text: The Enlightenment was an intellectual movement of the 1600s and 1700s that applied reason and scientific methods to human society, government, law, religion, and economics. It championed reason over tradition, evidence over superstition, and progress over the blind acceptance of inherited authority.

The Enlightenment grew directly out of the Scientific Revolution of the 1500s and 1600s, when thinkers like Copernicus, Galileo, and Isaac Newton showed the physical universe ran on consistent natural laws discoverable through reason. Enlightenment thinkers asked why reason could not also be applied to human society.

Enlightenment thinkers, often called philosophes in France, believed that just as natural laws governed physics, there were natural laws governing society and politics that humans could discover through reason, allowing them to sweep away ignorance and reform the world to be more just and free.

John Locke argued that all people are born with natural rights simply by being human: life, liberty, and property. These rights exist before government and cannot legitimately be taken away by any king.

The social contract is the idea that government is not divinely ordained but an agreement among people who consent to be governed in exchange for the protection of their rights. Legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed, not the will of God.

John Locke argued that if a government violates the people's natural rights and breaks the social contract, the people have the right to overthrow it. This 'right of revolution' became the philosophical justification beneath the revolutions of the period.

Jean-Jacques Rousseau advanced popular sovereignty, the principle that ultimate political authority belongs to the people themselves. He wrote about the social contract and the 'general will' of the people.

The Baron de Montesquieu developed the idea of separation of powers: dividing government into branches (legislative, executive, and judicial) that check one another to prevent tyranny. This idea was written directly into constitutions such as that of the United States.
Voltaire was the era's fierce champion of freedom of speech, freedom of religion, and toleration. He attacked censorship and the power of the Catholic Church, defending civil liberties.

Mary Wollstonecraft, in her Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), argued that if rights and reason were natural to humans, then women, being human, must possess them too. She demanded education and equality for women, extending Enlightenment logic.

Adam Smith argued for free markets and laissez-faire economics, the idea that economies work best when governments interfere little. His ideas became a foundation of modern capitalism and economic liberty.

Many Enlightenment thinkers were critical of the Catholic Church's power and of 'superstition,' favoring religious toleration. Some embraced deism, a stripped-down 'natural' religion based on reason rather than revelation or church authority.

In his Two Treatises of Government (1689), Locke argued for natural rights and the right of revolution. In 1776 Thomas Jefferson encoded these ideas almost verbatim in the American Declaration of Independence: unalienable rights, government by consent of the governed, and the people's right to alter or abolish a tyrannical government.

Enlightenment ideas spread through printed books, pamphlets, and newspapers, and through Diderot's Encyclopédie, which tried to gather all human knowledge in one rational reference work. Rising literacy and the printing press carried banned books across borders.

Enlightenment ideas circulated in social spaces like coffeehouses, lending libraries, and the salons hosted by elite women, where thinkers met and debated. The movement acted as an early information network carrying subversive ideas across Europe and the Atlantic.

The Enlightenment proclaimed that 'all men' had natural rights and were equal, but most male philosophers meant propertied European men. The gap between these universal promises and the narrow reality of who held rights became a central tension of the period.

Enlightenment ideas often stretched beyond their authors' intentions. Women, enslaved and free people of African descent, and colonized peoples seized the logic that all people are born with natural rights to argue that slavery, exclusion, and colonial subjugation could not be justified.

Throughout c. 1750–1900, reformers used the Enlightenment's own words against the societies that produced them: abolitionists demanding an end to slavery, women demanding the vote and education, and colonized peoples demanding freedom, all invoking natural rights and equality.

Enlightenment ideas were double-edged. The same reverence for reason and 'natural law' that justified human rights and democracy could be twisted to justify domination, as pseudo-scientific reasoning about human difference was later used to justify racism and imperialism.

The Enlightenment forged the modern vocabulary of politics: that governments should answer to the people, that individuals have rights no ruler can erase, that power should be limited and divided, and that authority must justify itself by reason. Nearly every revolution and reform movement of the period traces back to it.
